Annual removal now is the stored carbon divided by age (a simplification: it averages the tree's whole life).
The curve is the age-only Tier 1 scenario (curve_method tier1-age), so it can differ from the measured stored carbon at today's age.
Species allometry 'temperate_generic' has no verified equation yet; Chave et al. 2014 eq. 4 was applied outside its pantropical calibration domain.
No area was given, so the 4 trees are treated as a stand at the species' reference density of 400 trees per hectare (0.01 ha).

Carbon counted is above- plus below-ground tree biomass, expressed as CO2e; soil, litter and dead wood are not included.
Scenario estimate only: removals already made by existing trees are not carbon credits.

rules.name: CRCF carbon-farming certification methodologies (Commission Delegated Regulation, C(2026)4666, adopted 10 July 2026)
rules.summary: The Commission adopted certification methodologies for afforestation, agroforestry on mineral soils and peatland rewetting on 10 July 2026; until they enter into force, certification schemes cannot yet apply for recognition for these activities.
rules.details: The Commission news item of 10 July 2026 says the delegated act (C(2026)4666) covers agriculture and agroforestry on mineral soils, rewetting and restoration of peatlands and other organic soils, and afforestation, and that 'once the Delegated Regulation enters in force, certification schemes will be able to apply for recognition' under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2358. The news item and methodologies page opened do not state the methodologies' rules on existing trees, baselines, additionality or minimum monitoring period. Entry into force after Parliament and Council scrutiny was not confirmed as of 2026-10-05.

rules.notes: Status 'proposed' means adopted by the Commission but not confirmed in force. Still needed: the delegated act text and annexes to confirm whether pre-existing trees and biomass are baselined or credited, land-eligibility history, the standardised baseline and the minimum activity and monitoring periods. Third-party critiques of earlier drafts (Carbon Market Watch, March 2025: a zero standardised baseline with sparse existing trees on up to 10% of the area ignored; Bellona, 25 February 2026: pre-existing vegetation ignored with a zero baseline) are not evidence of the adopted text.
rules.why: Applies in the EU at any age (proposed, not yet in force; not yet confirmed from a primary source)

rules.name: Regulation (EU) 2024/3012 (CRCF): carbon farming, quantification, baseline and additionality
rules.authority: European Union: European Commission and recognised certification schemes
rules.summary: Under the EU's voluntary certification framework only net removals above a baseline from an activity lasting at least five years can be certified, and the activity must go beyond legal requirements and need the certification incentive.
rules.details: Article 2(10) defines carbon farming as 'any practice or process carried out over an activity period of at least five years, related to the management of a terrestrial or coastal environment' that results in carbon storage or lower soil emissions. Article 4 calculates the net carbon-farming benefit by subtracting baseline removals and associated emissions from total removals, preferring standardised baselines 'highly representative of the standard performance of comparable practices'. Article 5(1) requires that the activity goes 'beyond Union and national statutory requirements at the level of an individual operator' and needs 'the incentive effect of the certification' to be financially viable, and Article 5(2) presumes additionality when a standardised baseline is used. Article 6 requires monitoring for at least the activity period, with operators liable for releases during monitoring.

sources.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/3012 establishing a Union certification framework for permanent carbon removals, carbon farming and carbon storage in products
sources.publisher: EUR-Lex (Official Journal of the European Union)

rules.notes: The Regulation text read does not address existing carbon stocks explicitly; treating them as part of the baseline follows from Article 4's net-benefit formula. An Atlas estimate is never automatically CRCF-certifiable: certification by a recognised scheme is required. Article references were read through a page-summarising tool.
rules.why: Applies in the EU at any age

rules.name: Gold Standard Land Use & Forests Activity Requirements (A/R), v1.2.1, with A/R methodology v2.1
rules.summary: Gold Standard's afforestation and reforestation rules only cover planting on land that was not forest 10 years before the project start, so trees that already stand earn no credits.
rules.details: Activity Requirements v1.2.1 (April 2020), Section 2.1.1(b): 'The eligible area shall not meet the definition of forest 10 years before project start date and at project start date.' Credits are not issued for existing forests, improved forest management or avoided deforestation under these A/R requirements, and the A/R project start date is the earliest date when the first trees are planted. In A/R methodology v2.1 (16 May 2024, Section 3.5.1) the baseline is the 'tree' and 'non-tree' biomass present in the eligible planting area just prior to the planting start, and baseline trees are tracked inside the baseline.

rules.name: Verra VM0047 Afforestation, Reforestation and Revegetation, v1.1
rules.summary: VM0047 credits trees that a project plants or restores; the carbon already stored in pre-existing trees is measured as a starting (t=0) stock and is not credited.
rules.details: Area-based approach: project land must not have met the definition of managed forest at any point in the 10 years immediately preceding the project start date, although v1.1 also allows enhancing forest carbon stocks where existing forest cover has not been managed for wood products in the past ten years. A t = 0 carbon-stock estimate is required for pre-existing woody biomass, and removal of that biomass is only allowed where it is treated as a waste product with no commercial value. Census-based approach (dispersed planting such as agroforestry): planting density must not exceed 50 planting units per hectare, only direct planting is allowed, the pre-project land use must be maintained, and the area must have less than 10% pre-existing woody biomass cover (or be under continuous cropping, 'settlements' or 'other lands').

rules.name: Berliner Baumschutzverordnung (BaumSchVO)
rules.authority: Land Berlin: Umwelt- und Naturschutzämter of the district offices
rules.summary: Example: in Berlin, deciduous trees (except fruit trees), Scots pines, walnuts and Turkish hazels are protected once the trunk circumference is 80 cm at 1.30 m height, or 50 cm on at least one stem of a multi-stem tree; the test is size, not age.
rules.details: Protected are all deciduous trees except fruit trees, Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris) and, among fruit trees, walnut and Turkish hazel; a single-stem tree needs a trunk circumference of at least 80 cm and a multi-stem tree at least one stem of 50 cm, measured at 130 cm above the ground (directly under the crown if it starts lower). Felling, significant pruning and root interventions need an exemption permit, which the district office can grant only in the cases listed in section 5 of the ordinance and usually with conditions for replacement planting (Ersatzpflanzung) or a compensation payment (Ausgleichszahlung). Newly planted replacement trees are protected whatever their circumference.
rules.notes: Municipal example only: other German cities have their own Baumschutzsatzung with different thresholds. The ordinance text itself could not be read (the umwelt-online.de copy was unreadable), so details come from the Berlin service portal and a district office page, which also name the legal basis (BNatSchG sections 29(1) and 39(5) no. 2, BaumSchVO section 5, NatSchG Bln).
rules.why: Applies in Berlin (DE-BE) to urban trees at any age — a municipal example; check your own city's rules

rules.name: ICVCM Core Carbon Principles 5-7: additionality, permanence, robust quantification
rules.authority: Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM)
rules.summary: A carbon credit may only count removals that would not have happened without carbon revenue, so the growth that trees already standing would make anyway is not creditable on its own.
rules.details: Principle 5 (additionality): the emission reductions or removals 'shall be additional, i.e., they would not have occurred in the absence of the incentive created by carbon credit revenues.' Principle 6 (permanence): they 'shall be permanent or, where there is a risk of reversal, there shall be measures in place to address those risks and compensate reversals.' Principle 7: they 'shall be robustly quantified, based on conservative approaches, completeness and scientific methods.'

sources.title: Core Carbon Principles
sources.publisher: Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market

rules.notes: The plain-language reading for existing trees (growth that happens anyway is not additional, which is why methodologies use baselines) is the Atlas's interpretation of Principle 5, not ICVCM text. See docs/concepts/additionality.md.

rules.name: Guidelines for defining, mapping, monitoring and strictly protecting EU primary and old-growth forests (SWD(2023) 62 final)
rules.summary: Non-binding EU guidance tells Member States how to identify and strictly protect old-growth forests using structural indicators such as old or large trees and deadwood; it sets no numeric tree-age threshold.
rules.details: Section 2.3 (p. 7) defines old-growth forest as 'A forest stand or area consisting of native tree species that have developed, predominantly through natural processes, structures and dynamics normally associated with late-seral developmental phases in primary or undisturbed forests of the same type.' Section 3.2 lists seven indicators (three main, four complementary); the main ones include native species composition, a high proportion and diversity of standing and lying deadwood, and the 'presence of old or large trees, some of which may reach the maximum age known for the species'. The guidelines contain no numerical age threshold and are 'voluntary and not prescriptive', not a binding condition for state aid or EU funding.

rules.notes: Status 'in-force' here only means the guidance is published; it is not law. Protection of old-growth forests depends on Member State mapping and national or regional law.
